noteRef.topicTitle: The nature and variety of living organisms

specPoints.text: describe the common features shown by prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria Bacteria: these are microscopic single-celled organisms; they have a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm and plasmids; they lack a nucleus but contain a circular chromosome of DNA; some bacteria can carry out photosynthesis but most feed off other living or dead organisms. Examples include Lactobacillus bulgaricus , a rod-shaped bacterium used in the production of yoghurt from milk, and Pneumococcus , a spherical bacterium that acts as the pathogen causing pneumonia.

primer.text: Prokaryotes are the second great camp of living organisms, and bacteria are the examples this course cares about. This note fixes their shared cell plan — no enclosed nucleus, loose circular DNA, plasmids — and the two named species worth remembering, one that helps make yoghurt and one that causes pneumonia.

lessons.title: The prokaryote plan and the bacteria portrait
lessons.opening: Prokaryotes stand apart from every group in the previous note because their cells never enclose their genetic material in a nucleus. Bacteria are the prokaryotes this course names: microscopic, single-celled, and equipped with a wall, a membrane, cytoplasm and plasmids. Learning that portrait, plus the circular chromosome, covers the whole spec point.
keyPoints: Prokaryotic cells keep their genetic material loose in the cytoplasm instead of inside a nucleus.
Bacteria are microscopic single-celled organisms and are the named prokaryote examples.
A bacterial cell carries a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm and plasmids.
Bacteria lack mitochondria and any other membrane-bound organelles.
Lactobacillus bulgaricus helps turn milk into yoghurt; Pneumococcus causes pneumonia.

low.restatement: Prokaryotes: single cells with no nucleus; the DNA sits in the cytoplasm. Bacteria add a wall, membrane, cytoplasm and plasmids, with no mitochondria.
low.analogy: A prokaryotic cell is an open-plan studio: everything shares one room, with the chromosome lying in the open rather than locked in an office.
low.examPointer: Two marks hide in 'plasmids' and 'circular chromosome of DNA' — lists that omit them lose the detail marks.

medium.restatement: The prokaryotic signature is the absence of a membrane-bound nucleus and of any membrane-bound organelles; plasmids are separate small DNA loops that ride alongside the circular chromosome.
medium.analogy: Where a eukaryote keeps archives in labelled filing cabinets, a bacterium keeps one ring binder and a stack of loose cards (plasmids) on the same desk.
medium.examPointer: Comparisons that earn marks pair each prokaryotic absence with the eukaryotic presence: no nucleus versus enclosed nucleus, no mitochondria versus mitochondria present.

check.stem: Which structure does a bacterial cell LACK?

options.text: A nucleus enclosed by a membrane
options.explanation: Prokaryotes keep their DNA loose in the cytoplasm.
The wall is a named bacterial feature.
Plasmids are named bacterial DNA elements.
Cytoplasm is named as present.

check.stem: Which list gives the structures a bacterial cell POSSESSES?

options.explanation: Neither nucleus nor chloroplast exists here.

options.text: Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, plasmids
options.explanation: This is exactly the inventory the note lists.
No nucleus exists in bacteria.
Mitochondria are absent from bacteria.

check.stem: Why are bacteria described as prokaryotic rather than eukaryotic?

options.text: Because they lack a cell wall
options.explanation: They actually have a wall.
Lactobacillus is useful, so harm is not universal.

options.text: Because their genetic material sits loose in the cytoplasm with no enclosing membrane
options.explanation: The missing nucleus is the deciding contrast.
Size does not decide the classification.

check.stem: Which pairing of example bacterium and role is correct?

options.explanation: The two roles are swapped.
Mucor is a fungus, not a bacterium.
Yeast is a fungus and TMV is a virus.

options.text: Lactobacillus bulgaricus — yoghurt production; Pneumococcus — pneumonia
options.explanation: Both named examples pair correctly with their roles.

check.stem: What is the shape of the bacterial chromosome described in this note?

options.text: A single circular chromosome of DNA
options.explanation: The note names a circular chromosome.

options.text: Several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus
options.explanation: Both the shape and the location are wrong.
Plasmids ride alongside the main chromosome, they are not the whole genome.

options.text: No DNA at all, only RNA
options.explanation: Bacteria carry DNA; RNA-only describes some viruses.

check.stem: State where the genetic material of a prokaryotic cell is found.
check.modelAnswer: Loose in the cytoplasm, with no enclosing nuclear membrane.

check.stem: Name the extra DNA elements a bacterial cell carries besides its chromosome.
check.modelAnswer: Plasmids — small loops of DNA in the cytoplasm.

check.stem: Explain why mitochondria cannot be drawn on a labelled bacterial cell diagram.
check.modelAnswer: Bacteria lack mitochondria and every other membrane-bound organelle; their energy-releasing chemistry runs directly across the cell membrane and in the cytoplasm, so any diagram showing a mitochondrion has drawn a eukaryotic feature on a prokaryotic cell.

check.stem: A pupil's labelled bacterial cell diagram includes plasmids, a cell wall and a nucleus. The plasmids and wall are correct — what must change, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The nucleus must be removed and replaced by DNA loose in the cytoplasm (a circular chromosome), because bacteria are prokaryotes with no membrane-enclosed nucleus.

glossary.definition: An organism whose cells carry their genetic material loose in the cytoplasm, with no membrane-enclosed nucleus.
A small extra loop of DNA found in bacterial cells alongside the main circular chromosome.
